Why every frontend developer should learn Postman (even if you’re just starting)
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Photo by Compagnons on UnsplashWhen I first started learning frontend development, I thought my job was simple.
Learn HTML.
Learn CSS.
Learn JavaScript.
Build websites.
That’s it.
Then one day, I heard another word…
Postman.
Everyone kept saying:
“Test the API in Postman first.”
“Check the response in Postman.”
“The API works in Postman.”
And I was thinking…
“Why do frontend developers even need Postman?” 😭
If you’ve ever asked yourself the same question, this article is for you.
Let’s keep it simple.
No complicated tech talk.
First… What Is Postman?
Postman is a tool developers use to test APIs.
Instead of building an entire website just to see if an API works, you can test the API directly inside Postman.
Think of it like testing a TV remote.
Before blaming the TV, you first check whether the remote works.
That’s exactly what Postman helps developers do.
What Is an API?
Imagine you’re in a restaurant.
You tell the waiter what food you want.
The waiter takes your request to the kitchen.
The chef prepares your food.
The waiter brings it back.
The waiter is like an API.
The API carries your request and brings back the answer.
Postman simply helps you talk to that waiter.
Why Frontend Developers Need Postman
As a frontend developer, your website often needs information from somewhere else.
For example:

• weather information

• movie details

• football scores

• cryptocurrency prices

• news articles

• user accounts
That information usually comes from APIs.
Postman helps you see exactly what the API returns before you start writing code.
Imagine Building a Weather App
Let’s say you’re building a weather app.
Without Postman, you might spend hours writing code…
Only to discover the API isn’t working.
With Postman, you can test the API first.
If the API works, then you know your website can use it too.
That saves a lot of time.
What Can You Do in Postman?
Postman lets you:
✅ Send requests
✅ Receive responses
✅ Test APIs
✅ Check if data is correct
✅ Find problems before writing lots of code
Think of it as a practice area for APIs.
Understanding GET Requests
One of the first things beginners learn is the GET request.
GET simply means:
“I want some information.”
For example:
“Show me today’s weather.”
Or:
“Give me today’s football scores.”
That’s all GET does.
It asks for information.
Understanding POST Requests
POST means:
“I want to create something new.”
Examples:

• creating a new account

• sending a message

• posting a comment
You’re sending information instead of just asking for it.
What Is a Response?
After you send a request…
The API sends something back.
That’s called a response.
Imagine asking:
“What time is it?”
The answer you receive is the response.
Simple.
Why Testing First Is Important
Imagine buying a new phone charger.
Before charging your phone overnight…
You plug it in first to check if it works.
That’s exactly what Postman helps developers do.
It lets you test before building.
Common Beginner Mistakes
Thinking Postman Is Only for Backend Developers
Not true.
Frontend developers use Postman all the time.
Especially when working with APIs.
Ignoring the API Response
Many beginners only focus on writing code.
Instead…
First look at what the API returns.
Understanding the response makes writing your frontend much easier.
Being Afraid of JSON
When you first open Postman, you’ll probably see something called JSON.
Don’t panic 😄
JSON is simply a neat way of organizing information.
You’ll get comfortable with it through practice.
My Biggest Lesson
When I first heard about Postman, I thought it was another complicated developer tool.
Now I see it differently.
It’s simply a place where I can test APIs before connecting them to my projects.
That simple understanding made learning APIs much less stressful.
Final Thoughts
One thing I’ve learned during my frontend development journey is this:
The better you understand your tools…
The easier building projects becomes.
Postman isn’t just another application to install.
It’s a tool that helps you understand how your frontend communicates with APIs.
And that’s an important skill for every frontend developer.
If you’re learning web development, don’t skip Postman.
Spend some time exploring it.
Practice sending requests.
Read the responses.
The more you use it, the more confident you’ll become.
